why.core: A resume is the first thing an employer sees. It has to show, on one page, that you're reliable, you can learn and you'll turn up. You don't need work experience to do that. You need to turn the things you already do into skills, in words an employer understands.
why.extend: A resume is a tightly structured persuasive text read in moments by a stranger who must decide whether to call you. For a first job, the craft is translation: turning school, sport, family responsibilities and volunteering into precise, honest evidence of the qualities employers want.

articles.title: A resume with no experience

body.support:
Employers want to know three things. Will you **turn up**? Can you **learn**? Will you **get on** with people?

A first resume has six **sections**:

1. **Contact**: name, phone, email.
2. **Objective**: the job you want, in one line.
3. **Skills**: things you can do well.
4. **Experience**: things you've done. School, sport, helping out, family.
5. **Education**: your school and year.
6. **Referees**: two people who know you, like a coach. **Ask them first.**

Turn what you do into skills. *I play netball* becomes *Team member, netball, every Saturday.*

Start with a **doing word**: *served*, *helped*, *trained*.

Keep it **true**. Never make things up.
body.core:
Employers hiring for a first job aren't expecting years of experience. They want to know three things: Will you **turn up**? Can you **learn**? Will you **get on** with people? Your resume answers those questions on **one page**.

Most first resumes have six **sections**, in this order:

1. **Contact**: your name, phone number, email and suburb. Use a sensible email address.
2. **Objective**: one or two lines about the job you want. *A reliable, friendly Year 10 student looking for casual weekend work in hospitality.*
3. **Skills**: four to six skills, each with a short example.
4. **Experience**: anything that taught you something, paid or not. School roles, sport, volunteering, helping in a family business, looking after siblings.
5. **Education**: your school and year level, plus any certificates (first aid, food handling).
6. **Referees**: two people who know you, like a coach or teacher (not family). **Ask them first.**

The secret is **translation**. *I play netball* becomes *Team member, Under-17 netball, every Saturday for three years.* Start lines with **action verbs** (*served*, *organised*, *trained*, *looked after*) and add a **detail** that proves it: how often, how many, how long.

Keep it **honest**. Make true things sound strong, but never invent jobs, qualifications or referees. Employers check, and lying can cost you far more than the job.

Finally, **tailor** it. Read the job ad again and make sure your resume shows the essentials it asks for.
body.extend:
Employers hiring for first jobs aren't looking for experience. They want evidence that you're reliable, willing to learn and good with people. Your resume has to show that on **one page**.

Most first resumes follow six conventional **sections**:

1. **Contact**: name, phone, a professional email, suburb.
2. **Objective**: one or two lines, tailored to the job.
3. **Skills**: four to six, each with a short example.
4. **Experience**: paid or unpaid. School roles, sport, volunteering, family business and caring all count.
5. **Education**: school, year level and certificates (first aid, food handling).
6. **Referees**: two people who aren't family, asked first.

The core skill is **translation**: turning everyday activity into precise evidence. Start entries with **action verbs**, and add numbers where you can (*every Saturday for three years*, *a team of 12*). Cut repetition and vague words like *stuff* or *helped out*.

Keep it **honest**. Presenting real experience strongly is good practice. Inventing roles, qualifications or referees is deception, and it can have serious consequences.

Finally, **tailor** each version to the job ad, putting its essential criteria first.

caseStudies.title: The resume that went to court

body.support:
A woman named **Veronica Theriault** got a big government job in South Australia. It paid about **$270,000** a year.

But her resume was full of **lies**. Fake study. Fake jobs. She even **pretended to be her own referee** on the phone!

After about a **month**, they found out. She lost the job.

In **2019**, a court sent her to **jail** for 25 months.

The lesson: employers **check**. Make true things sound good. Never make things up.
body.core:
In **2017**, a woman named **Veronica Theriault** got a top job in the South Australian Government. It paid about **$270,000** a year.

She got it with a resume full of lies. It had **fake qualifications**, a made-up work history and false references. When the department rang her referee, she **pretended to be the referee** herself and gave herself a glowing review.

About a **month** after she started, the department found out something was wrong. She was dismissed.

She pleaded guilty to deception and other charges. In **December 2019**, she was sentenced to **25 months in jail**.

It's an extreme case. But the lesson works at every level: employers **check**. Make true things sound strong, and you'll never have to worry about what they find.
body.extend:
In **2017**, **Veronica Theriault** became chief information officer in South Australia's **Department of Premier and Cabinet**. The role paid around **$270,000** a year.

Her application used fake qualifications, a made-up work history and false references. When the department checked, she **pretended to be her own referee** and praised herself.

Within about a **month**, the department found problems and dismissed her. She pleaded guilty to deception and other charges. In **December 2019**, she was sentenced to **25 months' jail**.

The case is extreme, but it marks a line every resume writer should understand. Presenting real experience strongly is expected. Making things up is deception. Employers check, and the cost of being caught can be far worse than missing out on the job.

teacher.overview: Students write an honest one-page first resume. They learn its six conventional sections and how to translate everyday activities (sport, school roles, family responsibilities, volunteering) into skills, using action verbs and proving detail. The case study is the South Australian chief information officer jailed in 2019 for a fraudulent resume, which marks the line between strong framing and fabrication. Students peer-edit with a checklist, and the Level Up tailors the resume to a real job ad.
prep: Have a word-processing template ready if students will type their resume (one page, a plain font).
Optional: bring a real (anonymised) first resume, or your own from when you started.
Remind students to ask referees before listing them; a coach or teacher is ideal.

teacher.answers:
**Three things:** will you turn up; can you learn; will you get on with people. **Sections:** contact, objective, skills, experience, education, referees. Ask referees first so they're ready and willing.

**Resume:** 1 contact; 2 objective (one line, fits the job); 3 skill + proof; 4 experience (unpaid counts; duration shows reliability); 5 education + certificates; 6 referee (not family, asked first).

**Life → skills (samples):** footy — teamwork, commitment: *Team member, Under-17 footy, every weekend for four years*; market stall — customer service, cash handling: *Served customers and handled cash at a weekend market stall.*

**Power it up (samples):** *Use Word, Google Docs and Canva to create school assignments and posters.* / *Marked lanes and timed races at the school swimming carnival.* / *Supervised a group of six Year 7 students on school camp.*

**Case study:** fake qualifications, invented work history, false references; she impersonated her referee. Strong: *Served customers two lunchtimes a week*; made up: *Café supervisor* when you never were.

realityCheck: **“I've got nothing to write.”** Every student has something. Start by listing a normal week together; caring roles, part-time family work and sport are gold.
**Handle home lives with care.** Some students' responsibilities (caring for a parent, working in a family business) are private. They choose what goes on the page.
**Referees matter.** Students often list friends or family. Explain why a coach, teacher or manager is better, and have them ask first.
**The case study involves an adult's crime.** The court took her mental health into account at sentencing. Keep the discussion on the lesson (honesty, and that employers check), not on mocking her.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Students leave with a usable document, and it pairs naturally with Crack the Job Ad (before) and Nail the Interview (after).
